props.title: The Way I See It

sections.content: **The Way I See It** (2020) - not 2010 - offers unprecedented access to Pete Souza's intimate documentation of two pivotal American presidencies. As Chief White House Photographer for both Ronald Reagan and Barack Obama, Souza's lens captured watershed moments that parallel other significant political documentaries like The War Room (1993) and The Final Year (2017). The film particularly resonates with works like **All the President's Men** (1976) in how it reveals the machinery of American politics, though through still images rather than investigative journalism.

sections.content: The film's exploration of photography as both art and historical record connects strongly to other documentary works about photographers, particularly **Finding Vivian Maier** (2013) and Bill Cunningham New York (2010). What sets Souza's work apart is its intersection with power - his images don't just document moments, they shape how we remember entire presidencies. This approach to visual political history recalls **The Unknown Known** (2013), Errol Morris's probing examination of Donald Rumsfeld through interviews and archival footage.

Director Dawn Porter builds on her experience documenting civil rights issues in John Lewis: Good Trouble (2020), using Souza's evolution from neutral observer to outspoken critic as a lens for examining the role of truth and transparency in democracy. This transformation echoes themes found in **All the Truth to Tell** (2019) and **Shooting the Messenger** (2012), where documentation becomes an act of resistance. sections.content: The film's examination of how social media has transformed political imagery connects to broader discussions found in **The Social Dilemma** (2020) and **The Great Hack** (2019). Souza's Instagram-based resistance to what he saw as presidential norm-breaking represents a fascinating evolution in how political photographers engage with their subjects and the public. This shift mirrors themes explored in **Weiner** (2016), where political imagery and social media collide with dramatic consequences.
